I'm a 52-year-old farmer in Quzhou County with a good education, and I've been farming this land on the North China Plain for decades. I know my soil, I know the climate, and I know the market. My land is about 7 mu, and I run the standard double-cropping system that makes the most of every inch: winter wheat followed by summer maize. That's what the climate here allows, and that's where the stable demand is. The wheat is already in the ground from last October — it greens up in spring and I'll harvest it in early June. The day after harvest, I plant hybrid maize to catch the summer heat and long days, and I harvest that in late September or early October. 

Because I'm educated, I don't just copy what my neighbors do. I use improved wheat varieties like the Shimai or Liangxing lines and hybrid maize like Denghai or NK series — the seed cost pays itself back many times over in yield. For wheat, I rotary-till before sowing to get a good seedbed, and I apply about 16 kg of nitrogen, 8 kg of phosphorus, and 6 kg of potassium per mu, basing it on balanced fertilization rather than throwing on extra urea like some do. I irrigate three times at the critical stages: green-up or winter irrigation if dry, jointing, and grain filling. I spray three times — herbicide early, then insecticide and fungicide as needed. For maize, I go no-tillage right after wheat harvest to save time, fuel, and soil moisture. I give it about 16 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu, irrigate twice at the critical jointing and filling stages, and spray three times for weeds, pests, and disease control. I expect about 1,150 kg per mu of wheat and 1,300 kg per mu of maize if the weather holds. This system gives me two paychecks from the same plot every year, and with grain prices supported by government policy, it's the safest income I can count on.
